extracted.intended_audience: researchers and graduate students in philosophy of mathematics, logic, and game theory (those interested in Lakatos, paraconsistency, and formal epistemology)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and methodological criteria for carrying out and analysing Lakatos's Proofs and Refutations approach to mathematical discovery, especially insofar as it involves handling counterexamples, inconsistencies, and strategic (game-theoretic) responses. Focused on methods (monster-barring, lemma-incorporation, etc.), their game-theoretic interpretation, and paraconsistent/logical implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primitive conjecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with a primitive conjecture as the initial hypothesis or thesis that is to be examined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corfield’s step 1 in the summary of Lakatos’s method: the conjecture is the starting point for developing proofs, searching for counterexamples, and subsequent revisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof (rough thought experiment / decomposition into lemmas)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempt a proof as a rough thought experiment which decomposes the primitive conjecture into subconjectures and lemmas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corfield’s step 2: proofs are often rough and may rely on hidden lemmas; proof-analysis (making hidden lemmas explicit) is important for later scrutiny and revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Global counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify global counterexamples that refute the main conjecture (not just local lemmas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corfield’s step 3 and many examples in PR (e.g., nested cubes) — searching for counterexamples is a central strategic move that drives theory revision and discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof re-examined / guilty lemma spotted
rubrics_metrics.description: When a counterexample is found, re-examine the proof to spot the ‘guilty’ lemma that failed or was misidentified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corfield’s step 4: locating the faulty lemma allows targeted revision (rather than throwing away the whole proof) and is central to Lakatosian methodology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine other theorems for lemma occurrence
rubrics_metrics.description: Check proofs of other theorems to see whether the newly found guilty lemma occurs elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corfield’s step 5: this helps understanding the broader impact of the correction and whether revising the lemma affects other results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check previously accepted consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify hitherto accepted consequences of the original (now refuted) conjecture for further inconsistencies or required revisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corfield’s step 6: ensure dependent results are examined and adjusted if necessary — part of the iterative revision process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turn counterexamples into new examples / open new fields
rubrics_metrics.description: Transform counterexamples into new examples or domains of inquiry, thereby generating new research directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corfield’s step 7 and Lakatosian heuristic: counterexamples can be productive, leading to concept-stretching, new definitions, and new research programmes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monster-barring
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat a putative counterexample as a ‘monster’ (pathological case) and exclude it from the domain to preserve the theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lakatos’s method: when someone labels a nested-cube or similar object a monster, they argue it isn’t a genuine example of the kind the conjecture quantifies over; used strategically to maintain the theorem but criticized for being ad hoc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception-barring
rubrics_metrics.description: List and exclude exceptions to the conjecture so the conjecture persists over a restricted, ‘safe’ domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lakatosian technique: exception-barring retreats into a privileged field by excluding problematic cases; the method is conservative but may miss broader generalisations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of surrender
rubrics_metrics.description: Abandon the refuted conjecture and adopt a radically new approach when a counterexample convincingly undermines it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exemplified by GAMMA’s move in PR: when a counterexample is accepted as global, the rational move may be to surrender the conjecture and seek a new theory rather than patching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma-incorporation
rubrics_metrics.description: Respond to a global counterexample by adding an appropriate lemma (or condition) to the conjecture/proof-analysis so the improved conjecture incorporates that lemma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of Rule 2 in PR’s heuristic: make hidden lemmas explicit and replace the discarded conjecture by an improved one that incorporates the lemma; a central Lakatosian repair strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofs that do not prove (productive failed proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise that proofs which fail ('proofs that do not prove') can still be epistemically valuable by signalling errors or leading to lemmas and concept refinement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such failed proofs are central to Lakatos’s method and to the argument for paraconsistency: they supply signals (guilty lemmas), drive revisions, and may be costly but informative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy pruning / re-examining proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Prune strategies (or proofs) by removing alternatives known not to work, improving the strategy for subsequent runs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compared to iterated pruning in game theory: re-running and refining proofs or strategies is an evolutionary/game-theoretic move; it is analogous to removing dominated options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies (analogue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use iterated elimination of dominated strategies as a model for successive refinement of proof-strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lakatosian re-examination of proofs can be mapped to this game-theoretic solution method: successive eliminations refine the strategy space and proof attempts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revising proofs as strategy revision (self-reference issue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow strategies (proof plans) to be revised in light of opponents’ moves or new information, acknowledging the resulting self-reference and infinite-regress problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lakatosian practice entails revising proofs after new moves; formally this conflicts with the standard definition of a fixed strategy and raises epistemic/game-theoretic self-reference concerns (Harsanyi, Heifetz).

rubrics_metrics.name: Turning contradictions into new examples / meta-model updates
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat contradictions as opportunities: update the meta-model or definitions (lemma-incorporation, model revision) so inconsistencies become consistencies in a revised framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lakatosian heuristic and belief-revision parallels: counterexamples drive model change (e.g., turning a counterexample into an example by refining definitions), seen as a meta-model theoretical strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monster-adjustment
rubrics_metrics.description: Reinterpret or ‘adjust’ the perception/definition so that a putative monster becomes a legitimate example (therapeutic reinterpretation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RHO-style move in PR: rather than excluding the object, teach how to see/define it so it counts as an ordinary example (evolutionary/game-theoretic reinterpretation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of proof and refutations (three heuristic rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Heuristic rules: (1) set out to prove and to refute, prepare proof-analysis and find both global and local counterexamples; (2) if global counterexample, discard conjecture and add refuted lemma as condition to improved conjecture; (3) if local counterexample, check whether it’s global and apply rule 2 if so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lakatos’s stated rules (Rule 1–3) summarise a recursive strategy for discovery: explicit proof-analysis, responsive modification, and systematic checking of counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not-everything-goes constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain that from an identified inconsistency not everything should legally follow; the methodology constrains which inferences are permitted after contradictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Central to the claim that PR is paraconsistent: the method provides specific strategies (monster-barring, lemma-incorporation, etc.) to control consequences of contradictions, so the theory does not 'explode'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paraconsistent game elements (allow contradictory strategies, irrational players, non-classical probabilities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define paraconsistent games as games where under contradictions players can make rational moves; such games may allow contradictory strategies (leading to both win and loss), irrational players, and non-classical probabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper distinguishes epistemic and behavioural paraconsistent games and notes that such features are familiar from game semantics and evolutionary/behavioural game theory; these are permissible moves in a paraconsistent analysis of PR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistemic paraconsistent games
rubrics_metrics.description: Paraconsistent games concerning what players know: players’ epistemic states may be inconsistent but still yield rational strategic behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focuses on knowledge/belief aspects — e.g., patients of inconsistent information may still compute strategies; connects to epistemic game theory and belief revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioural paraconsistent games
rubrics_metrics.description: Paraconsistent games concerning inconsistent strategies and moves — behaviour may systematically deviate from classical rationality but can be modelled and explained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Links to behavioural game theory and experimental findings (Ariely, Kahneman): agents can be rational in the sense of goal-directed, even when acting on inconsistent beliefs or preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement: agents compute responses under uncertainty / know when equilibrium reached
rubrics_metrics.description: Players/agents should be able to compute their responses under uncertainty or imperfect information and recognise when the game has reached a solution or equilibrium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the proposed solution for PR-as-game: rationality requires computable responses and criteria for termination (equilibrium) so strategic handling of inconsistencies is feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost/limit to concept-stretching (terminate games)
rubrics_metrics.description: Impose a non-zero cost on unlimited concept-stretching to avoid destroying meaning and truth; ensure games/heuristics terminate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lakatos’s observation: unlimited concept-stretching destroys meaning; so protocols should penalise or limit too-flexible revisions (a metatheoretic constraint preventing endless adjustments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-classical negation and non-zero-sum outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow logics and games where proving a proposition does not entail the opponent's negation (¬ϕ may still hold); winning need not be zero-sum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In PR, defending a conjecture and refuting counterexamples can be compatible; non-classical negation and non-zero-sum semantics (Hintikka-style) accommodate this feature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for 'cheaper' proofs (resource-aware rationality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agents may prefer proofs that use fewer computational resources (time, memory, processor), treating resource cost as part of their utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A pragmatic/game-theoretic desideratum: computational cost influences strategic choices — e.g., pick proofs that are 'cheaper' if they suffice, akin to bounded-rationality considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bracketing / exclusion of inconsistent information (Hintikka’s IMI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude (bracket) pieces of information from epistemic reasoning that would produce contradictions, choosing strategically what to ignore.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hintikka’s interrogative model of inquiry uses bracketing as a deliberate strategy; selection of what to bracket must be strategic and can be seen as a game move.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat: elimination of conjuncts causes information loss / may be infeasible
rubrics_metrics.description: Be wary of eliminating conjuncts to restore consistency because this may lose important information and sometimes identifying the trouble-maker conjunct is impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of simple belief-revision/elimination strategies: removing a conjunct to resolve contradiction may have informational costs and theoretical limits (Priest’s and others’ objections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of alternative logical operators (non-classical conjunctions/conditionals) as repair
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain information and avoid trivialisation by employing different conjunctions or conditionals (e.g., multiplicative conjunctions, magic-wand) rather than eliminating conjuncts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logical pluralism and technical devices can preserve more content while handling contradictions; an alternative to outright elimination in classical belief-revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paraconsistent acceptance criterion (quasi-truth / comparative preference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept an inconsistent (quasi-true) theory rationally if it is sufficiently better than competitors on sufficiently many criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bueno & da Costa’s thesis: rational agents may entertain inconsistent theories if those theories perform better overall — a comparative criterion for acceptance under paraconsistency.
